title: Added exposure curves gave no clear interaction change in four US bird samples in 1995-2024
abstract: We tested whether curved ozone and temperature responses changed an ozone by warmth estimate for recorded bird species. We used a signed public-data panel and kept the same surveys and controls in each comparison. Four samples covered eastern and western US routes in 1995-2009 and 2010-2024. Added squared exposure anomalies removed 9-23% of the product variation left after the original controls. Interaction changes ranged from -0.209 to +0.247 recorded species per 10 ppb per 2 C. All four multiple-test intervals included zero. One uncorrected interval excluded zero. Cubic terms gave no clear repeated change. Thus, curved responses share some model information with the product term, but these data do not establish a change in its coefficient. Few western state clusters, selected monitor coverage, exposure error and unmeasured detection changes limit inference. This is a model check, not a causal test or evidence that ozone is safe.

display.caption: Left: interaction estimates and marginal 95% state-cluster intervals. Right: paired changes after squared exposure terms, with four-test Bonferroni intervals. Units are recorded species per 10 ppb per 2 C. Every corrected change interval includes zero.

citations.reason: Verified source of the unchanged complete-case survey panel, original code, estimates and raw-source provenance. Our question is sensitivity to additive exposure curves. This is not new independent field data.
Original public BBS, EPA ozone and NOAA climate panel construction, inherited through the immediate source.
Explains how correlated predictors and omitted curved responses can affect product terms in ecological models.
Prior evidence on air quality rules and bird abundance. Our observational recorded-richness model does not replicate its policy design.
